Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-3\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}\left({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right) & =0 \\ {\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}.
$$

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{i}) & =\mathbf{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{j}) & =\mathbf{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot \mathbf{i}$ and $T\cdot \mathbf{j}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{i}) & =T\cdot \mathbf{i}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{j}) & =T\cdot \mathbf{j}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-3\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}\left({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}=0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right) & =0 \\ {\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}

$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}=0.

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right) & =0 \\ {\left(\lambda -\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y=A{e}^{3x/2}+Bx{e}^{3x/2}.

differences.stored:

differences.source:
The square root of a squared quantity can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\sqrt{{x}^{2}}=|x|
$$

In our case, we can simplify the given expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{100{a}^{2}} &= \sqrt{{(10a)}^{2}} \\ &= |10a| \\ &= |10|\cdot |a| \\ &= 10\cdot |a|\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $a<0.$ To take the absolute value of any negative number we need to flip the sign, so we have $|a|=-a.$ Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}10\cdot |a| &= 10\cdot (-a) \\ &= -10a.\end{aligned}
$$
